summary: Implement a LIFO stack using only queue operations.
mainInsight: A queue is FIFO, so make the newest element reach the front by rotating the queue after each push: push x, then move the previous n elements behind it. Pop and top are then plain queue operations.

approaches.name: Two queues, costly pop
approaches.summary: Push O(1); pop moves n-1 elements to a helper queue.

approaches.name: One queue, costly push
approaches.summary: After pushing, rotate the queue n-1 times so the new element is at the front.

personalSolution.notes: Valid and common. Mention the one-queue costly-pop alternative.

promptVariants: How do you get LIFO from a FIFO queue?
What operation makes the newest element dequeue first?
options: Rotate the queue so the newest element is at the front
Sort the queue by insertion time after every push call
Reverse the queue by recursion on each pop call only
Use a heap ordered by insertion time to pop the newest first
cards.answer: Rotate the queue so the newest element is at the front
cards.explanation: Moving the previous elements behind the new one reverses their relative order to LIFO.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Reverse the queue by recursion on each p: Recursion needs a stack frame, which defeats the purpose.

promptVariants: What is the invariant of your queue after each push?
Why does rotating n-1 times work?
cards.answer: The front of the queue is always the most recently pushed element, with older elements behind it in LIFO order. After appending x, rotate the n-1 older elements (pop from the front, append to the back) so they sit behind x and x is at the front.
keyPoints: Rotate the older elements behind the new one
cards.explanation: That cost is paid once per push.

promptVariants: Time of push in the one-queue rotation approach (n elements): ___
Complete the statement: Time of push in the one-queue rotation approach (n elements): ___
What is the space complexity and the trade-off between making push or pop expensive?
Which costs can you trade in Stack-using-Queues and what is the space?
cards.answer: O(n) for the single queue. You can choose push O(n)/pop O(1) (yours) or push O(1)/pop O(n); amortised O(1) for both is not possible with queues alone in this design.
cards.explanation: Pick based on the expected operation mix.

promptVariants: Trace push(1), push(2), push(3). What does the queue look like after each push?
Show the queue contents after each of push(1), push(2), push(3) in the rotating-queue stack.
cards.answer: [1] -> append 2 gives [1,2], rotate once -> [2,1] -> append 3 gives [2,1,3], rotate twice -> [3,2,1]. The front is always the latest push.

promptVariants: What should top() return on an empty stack according to the constraints?
How does your code treat it?
options: Constraints guarantee non-empty top/pop; the guard is only a safety net
It must raise an exception when the stack is empty on top
It must return -1 as a sentinel when the stack is empty
It should rebuild the queue from scratch before returning
cards.answer: Constraints guarantee non-empty top/pop; the guard is only a safety net
cards.explanation: LeetCode only calls pop/top on non-empty stacks, so any guard value is arbitrary.
